# Abstract

This paper introduces diffusion network research and presents an R library, netdiffuseR, that facilitates the estimation of contagion and diffusion processes on networks. Diffusion of innovations theory explains how new ideas and practices spread within and between communities. The spreading process consists of person-to-person interactions in which adopters persuade (by whatever means) non-adopters to adopt. Estimating these effects requires network data and an indicator for when each person adopts. The analytic steps involve creating an event history version of the data set and regression estimation to determine if exposure, the adopters in one’s network, is associated with individual adoption. netdiffuseR automates many of these data management and processing steps, thus facilitating the estimation of these models. The package also contains simple ways to compute various network exposure measures such as based on structural equivalence, indirect ties, homophilic ties, etc. In addition, netdiffuseR provides capabilities to conduct simulations of network diffusion processes varying network structure, seed conditions, threshold distributions, and influence mechanisms. The paper includes example code for both empirical and simulated network studies. We aim to facilitate the adoption of netdiffuseR to advance the growth and evolution of diffusion network research. 

# Introduction

This paper provides a general overview of the R package netdiffuseR, a library for estimating contagion and diffusion processes on networks. We provide a brief introduction to diffusion of innovations theory, introduce netdiffuseR, present a tutorial for empirical work, and give examples of simulations. We also describe ways to analyze the simultaneous diffusion of multiple behaviors, such as the adoption of complementary or competing products. Lastly, we demonstrate how to model disadoption. This paper enables researchers to use the netdiffuseR package to read, analyze, visualize, and simulate diffusion networks.

Diffusion of innovations is a theoretical approach that explains how new ideas and practices spread within and between communities. Diffusion of innovations theory has been used to study the spread of: fertility preferences and contraceptive choices [@bongaarts_social_1996; @valente_social_1997]; risk behaviors such as smoking [@christakis_spread_2007]; alcohol use [@light_onset_2013]; substance use [@hoffman_peer_2006; @fujimoto_alcohol_2013]; physician behavior [@Coleman1966; @iyengar_opinion_2011]; public health policies [@valente_diffusion_2015; @yamagata2017]; physical activity [@aral_exercise_2017]; among other behaviors. Thus, developing a platform to easily analyze and compare factors associated with network influences on adoption has broad applicability in the behavioral and physical sciences.

Diffusion theory states that a new idea or practice enters a community or population from some external source such as an impersonal medium, a person from another community, or a technological shift [@rogers_diffusion_2003; @valente_origins_1995].  The idea or practice then spreads from person to person through interpersonal communication. Thus, the theory and techniques of social network analysis are integral to the study of the diffusion of innovations [@valente_social_2010], and constitute the field of diffusion networks.

The workhorse variable used to measure network influences on adoption is network exposure which is the number or proportion of adopters in a person’s immediate social network contemporaneously or lagged by one (or more) time periods (which depending on the study could be days, months, or years). The formula for the lagged exposure model is:

$$
E_{it} = \frac{\sum_{j\neq i}W_{ij}a_{j(t-1)}}{\sum_{j\neq i}W_{ij}}
$$

Here, $W_{ij}$ is a weight matrix indicating ties between individuals, most commonly a binary adjacency matrix such as a friendship network, although it can represent any relation. The adoption vector $a$ indicates which of person $i$'s alters $j$ had adopted at time $t - 1$, and the denominator is the row sum, or number of outgoing ties. $E_{it}$ in Equation 1 measures the proportion of a person's ties at time $t$ who had adopted the behavior by the prior time period. As described in @Valente2024, the exposure calculation can be extended by using a count (removing the denominator) or by weighting ties according to indirect connectivity, structural equivalence, strength (weak versus strong), homophily, Simmelian relations (alter-to-alter), or alter network properties such as centrality. The `exposure()` function enables users to calculate these alternatives through its arguments.

There are other measures needed to estimate diffusion network effects. A network threshold [@valente_threshold_1996] is the proportion or number of adopters in an individual's network required for that individual to adopt. Although the observed exposure at adoption may coincide with this threshold, interval-based observation can make exposure overstate it. For example, a person whose threshold is two may be observed only after three peers adopted during the same interval; the observed exposure is then three even though the threshold was two [see @berryOpacityProblemSocial2019 for a detailed discussion].

Some people innovate with none or few adopters in their network adopting whereas others wait until a majority or all adopt. Network thresholds provide a means to estimate the classic two-step flow hypotheses [@katz_two-step_1957] and have been shown to moderate health promotion impacts [@valente_mass_1998]. In addition, the threshold distribution drives the diffusion rate and prevalence [@valente_yon_2020]. Other diffusion network measures are Moran’s I, a measure of contagion, network susceptibility, network influence [@valente_diffusion_2015], the hazard rate, and Bass model parameter coefficients [@bass_new_1969; @valente_diffusion_1993].

# The netdiffuseR package

The netdiffuseR R package [@valente_yon_2020; @netdiffuser_2] was first released to CRAN on February 18, 2016. The package contains a collection of algorithms and methods first envisioned by Dr. Valente and released as GAUSS code with his book [@valenteNetworkModelsDiffusion1995].

In a nutshell, netdiffuseR provides methods for simulating, processing, analyzing, and visualizing diffusion networks. Among its key functions are the `survey_to_diffnet()` function, `rdiffnet()` function, and the `exposure()` function. The `survey_to_diffnet()` function provides an interface to read in tabular data (in R `data.frame` format) corresponding to survey data containing network nominations and time of adoption [TOA]. The function makes it easy to process survey data, pass multiple checks, and build the adoption and cumulative adoption matrices. The `rdiffnet()` function allows simulating diffusion networks using the threshold model and, since version 1.23.0, simulating multi-diffusion and disadoption. Users can simulate diffusion processes on pre-defined networks or random graphs in a computationally efficient way. Finally, the `exposure()` function–the workhorse of the R package–provides a flexible framework for calculating various types of exposure measures as indicated above. In the following section of the paper, we will provide a demonstration of these functions.

# A tutorial on netdiffuseR

This tutorial was developed using **R** version 4.5.1 [@R], **Quarto** version 1.6.42 [@Allaire_Quarto_2025], and **netdiffuseR** version 1.25.0. The multi-adoption and disadoption features demonstrated below were introduced in netdiffuseR version 1.23.0 and are available in the current CRAN release. Readers can find the Quarto document and all materials required to reproduce the paper at <https://github.com/gvegayon/netdiffuser-connections>.

## Analyzing existing data

First, we will show how to read survey data into netdiffuseR. We start by loading the package. If you don't have the package installed in your system, you can use the `install.packages()` function:

```r
install.packages("netdiffuseR")
```

Notice that this is required to do only once. The previous code will install the package in your R system, but it will not load it. Once you are sure the package is available in your computer, you can use the function `library()` to load it:

```{r}
#| label: first-look
# Loading the netdiffuseR
suppressPackageStartupMessages(
  suppressWarnings(library(netdiffuseR))
)
```

The package includes three classical diffusion datasets that we can use as a starting point. Here, we use the Korean Family Planning study [@rogers_book_1981]. Let us first inspect the data using the `data()`, `dim()`, and `str()` functions. The `data()` function loads datasets from R packages, `dim()` reports their dimensions, and `str()` summarizes their structure:

```{r}
#| label: loading-kfamily
# Loading the dataset and taking a look
# at the data structure
data(kfamily)
dim(kfamily) # Number of rows and columns
str(kfamily[,1:10]) # structure of the first 10 columns
```

::: {.callout-tip}
You can always inspect datasets that are included in an R package using the `data()` function. For example, in netdiffuseR, you can use `data(package="netdiffuseR")`.
:::

As you can see, the dataset contains 1,047 observations with 432 columns. The dataset consists of survey data collected in 1973-1974 from women of childbearing age in 25 rural villages. For this example, we will focus on the two largest villages, namely villages 2 and 21. We can subset the data using the following code:

```{r}
kfamily <- subset(kfamily, village %in% c(2, 21))

# These identifiers and time variables represent whole numbers.
# Converting them explicitly prevents coercion warnings below.
kfamily[c("id", "village", "toa")] <- lapply(
  kfamily[c("id", "village", "toa")],
  as.integer
)
```

The survey has multiple network nomination questions. Depending on the situation, one may aggregate them or focus on one relation. We use the “talks to a neighbor” question, for which participants nominated up to five people. We then use `survey_to_diffnet()` to create a `diffnet` object:

```{r}
# Reading in the data
kfam_diffnet <- survey_to_diffnet(
  dat      = kfamily,
  idvar    = "id",
  netvars  = c("net11", "net12", "net13", "net14", "net15"),
  toavar   = "toa",
  groupvar = "village"
)
```

The key points are: (1) `idvar` identifies each individual in the dataset; (2) `netvars` lists the network-nomination columns; (3) `toavar` identifies the time-of-adoption variable, measured in years here; and (4) because the data contain multiple communities, `groupvar` specifies that ties can occur within but not between villages. The function has additional options documented in `?survey_to_diffnet`.

R distinguishes between numeric values stored as decimals and values stored as integers. The identifiers, village codes, and adoption years in this example are whole numbers, so we converted them explicitly with `as.integer()` before calling `survey_to_diffnet()`. This prevents the coercion warnings that would otherwise appear without changing the values.

The terminal time category in the Korean Family Planning data requires special treatment. Period 11 does not represent a regular observation wave: instead, it assigns an adoption time to every respondent who had not adopted in an earlier period. If these assignments were treated as observed adoptions, cumulative prevalence would be forced to 100%, which could bias analyses of the diffusion process. In the two villages used here, 51 respondents receive this terminal code. We treat them as right-censored by replacing their time of adoption with `NA`, and then use the `diffnet` subsetting method to remove period 11. The resulting object contains the ten genuinely observed periods and a final observed prevalence below 100%:

```{r}
#| label: remove-terminal-period
# Identify respondents assigned to the terminal time category.
terminal_period <- max(kfam_diffnet$meta$pers)
terminal_cases <- diffnet.toa(kfam_diffnet) == terminal_period

# Treat their adoption times as right-censored.
diffnet.toa(kfam_diffnet)[terminal_cases] <- NA_integer_

# Retain only the genuinely observed network periods.
kfam_diffnet <- kfam_diffnet[, , kfam_diffnet$meta$pers < terminal_period]
```

The `diffnet` object we just created has several inspection methods. `print()` gives a glimpse of the data, including the number of time points and nodes, network type, and adoption prevalence. `summary()` describes the adoption dynamics, including the number and proportion of adopters at each time point, network density, and Moran’s I [@moran_1950] as a measure of spatial autocorrelation. Finally, `plot_diffnet()` visualizes the diffusion process by coloring nodes as non-adopters, new adopters, or continuing adopters. The following code chunk demonstrates the first two functions:

```{r}
#| label: diffnet-methods
print(kfam_diffnet) # Using print() is not necessary, but recommended.
summary(kfam_diffnet)
```

::: {.callout-tip}
By default, Moran’s I is computed using the inverse of the geodesic-distance matrix. The `moran()` function also supports other weighting matrices.
:::

Because the network layout is stochastic, we use `set.seed()` immediately before plotting to make the figure reproducible:

```{r}
#| label: diffnet-plot-method
set.seed(33)
plot_diffnet(kfam_diffnet)
```

Of the observed outcomes, it is noteworthy that (a) the diffusion process is apparent in the figure, with adoptions occurring from the core toward the periphery of the graph, and (b) Moran’s I shows a high level of spatial autocorrelation between periods four and ten. Other visualization functions include `plot_diffnet2()`, `plot_threshold()`, `plot_adopters()`, and `plot_infectsuscept()`. We invite readers to learn more about them in the netdiffuseR manual.

## Computing exposures

Exposures are a fundamental part of estimating diffusion network effects. Consequently, netdiffuseR provides a wide range of possibilities when it comes to calculating exposures. Using the `exposure()` function, users can calculate cohesion (direct ties) and structural equivalence exposures [@burt_1987], attribute weighted exposure, tie-weighted exposure, count exposure (instead of proportion), and many more. The following code blocks show how to calculate three different types of exposure:

\noindent
**Cohesive exposure.** This is the simplest type of exposure: the proportion of neighbors who have adopted at each time point. The `exposure()` function returns an $n \times T$ matrix, where $n$ is the number of nodes and $T$ is the number of time points:

```{r}
#| label: computing-exposures-cohesive
exp_cohesive <- exposure(kfam_diffnet)

# Showing the exposure for the first five agents
# and first six time points
exp_cohesive[1:5, 1:6]
```

\noindent
**Structural equivalence.** This type of exposure is useful when influence may operate through similarity in network position rather than only through direct connections. An individual may be more likely to adopt a behavior when others occupying similar network positions adopt.

```{r}
#| label: computing-exposures-se
exp_se <- suppressMessages(suppressWarnings(
  exposure(kfam_diffnet, alt.graph = "se", valued = TRUE)
))

# Showing the exposure for the first five agents
# and first six time points
exp_se[1:5, 1:6]
```

Structural-equivalence scores are valued rather than binary, so we specify `valued = TRUE`. With some versions of the `Matrix` package, this calculation also produces an internal deprecation warning about coercing a `dgeMatrix` to a `dgCMatrix`. The warning does not indicate a problem with the calculated exposure, so the example suppresses this known internal warning explicitly.

\noindent
**Attribute weighted.** Finally, this type of exposure can be used when a characteristic of adopters may make them more influential in the social contagion process. For example, people may be more influenced by older individuals than younger:

```{r}
#| label: computing-exposures-attr
exp_age <- exposure(kfam_diffnet, attrs = "age")

# Showing the exposure for the first five agents
# and first six time points
exp_age[1:5, 1:6]
```

We can look at the three different exposures we just calculated by combining them into a single matrix. The following code chunk takes the fifth column (exposure at the fifth time point) and shows the exposures for the first ten individuals in the network:

```{r}
#| label: visualizing-exposures
# Visualizing exposure at time 5
cbind(
  "Cohesion"       = exp_cohesive[, 5],
  "SE"             = exp_se[, 5],
  "Attr. weighted" = exp_age[, 5]
) |> head(n = 10)
```

In addition to `exposure()`, netdiffuseR includes functions that can be combined with its core tools. For instance, we can use `vertex_covariate_compare()` to calculate age-homophilic exposure. Define an age-similarity weight as $s_{ij} = (1 + \lVert x_i-x_j\rVert)^{-1}$. Adding one keeps the weight finite and gives equal-age alters the maximum weight of one. The resulting exposure is:

$$
E_{it} = \frac{\sum_{j\neq i} W_{ij}a_{jt}s_{ij}}{\sum_{j\neq i} W_{ij}s_{ij}},
\qquad
s_{ij} = \frac{1}{1 + \lVert x_i-x_j\rVert}.
$$

Here, $\lVert x_i-x_j\rVert$ is the L2 distance between the ages of individuals $i$ and $j$. The following code uses `vertex_covariate_compare()` to generate an age-distance graph. Because the `graph` argument requires a single adjacency matrix, we pass the first graph in `kfam_diffnet`:

```{r}
#| label: age-homophilic-exp
# Using homophilic distance
age_distance_graph <- vertex_covariate_compare(
  # Passing the first graph
  graph   = kfam_diffnet$graph[[1]],
  # Passing the age parameter
  X       = kfam_diffnet[["age"]],
  funname = "distance"
)
```

The expression `kfam_diffnet$graph[[1]]` accesses the first network in the `diffnet` object, while `kfam_diffnet[["age"]]` extracts the `age` attribute. We can inspect the first few entries of the distance matrix:

```{r}
#| label: age-homophilic-exp-glimpse
age_distance_graph[1:10, 1:10]
```

We next convert distance to similarity and retain weights only for observed network ties. Multiplication by the original adjacency matrix ensures that non-ties remain zero, while the $1/(1+d)$ transformation assigns equal-age ties a weight of one:

```{r}
#| label: preparing-data
# Transforming age distance into similarity on observed ties
exp_age_homo_graph <- kfam_diffnet$graph[[1]] *
  (1 / (1 + as.matrix(age_distance_graph)))

exp_age_homo <- exposure(
  kfam_diffnet,
  alt.graph = exp_age_homo_graph,
  valued = TRUE
)
```

The warning from `exposure()` explains that the static alternative graph will be repeated for all $T$ time points. This is intentional: the Korean Family Planning example uses the same observed nomination network throughout the study. The next code chunk gives a glimpse of the exposure values we have calculated:

```{r}
#| label: showing-all-exposures
# Visualizing exposure at time 5
cbind(
  "Cohesion"       = exp_cohesive[, 5],
  "SE"             = exp_se[, 5],
  "Attr. weighted" = exp_age[, 5],
  "Homophilic"     = exp_age_homo[, 5]
) |> head(10)
```

In sum, the `exposure()` function provides considerable flexibility for calculating a wide range of exposures. Computing exposures is a fundamental task in the study of diffusion networks. A more in-depth treatment is given in [@Valente2024].

## Fitting a lagged exposure model

A natural step after computing exposures is estimating lagged exposure models. A common approach is a discrete-time logistic regression that predicts adoption as a function of node characteristics and lagged exposure. The `diffreg()` function facilitates this analysis. When `exposure` is included as a bare term, `diffreg()` automatically uses a one-period lag. The following code fits a baseline model using that default:

```{r}
#| label: diffreg
#| warning: true
model_baseline <- diffreg(kfam_diffnet ~ exposure)
summary(model_baseline)
```

The `diffreg()` function is a wrapper around R's `glm()` function. It expands the data into person-period observations and retains each person only while they are at risk of adopting, analogous to a discrete-time event-history analysis. Adoption at time $t$ is modeled using network exposure at time $t-1$. Because the predictor is lagged, one person's adoption at time $t$ is not used contemporaneously to predict another person's adoption at the same time. Under the usual conditional-independence assumptions of the specified logistic regression, the model can therefore be estimated using standard GLM inference; the fact that exposure is computed from a network does not by itself invalidate the regression. As in other regression settings, researchers may add fixed effects, random effects, or other adjustments when their substantive design requires them.

The baseline exposure coefficient is 0.606 on the log-odds scale ($p = 0.107$). Thus, a 0.10 increase in the proportion of adopting contacts is associated with a multiplicative change of $\exp(0.10 \times 0.606) = 1.06$ in the odds of adoption, or approximately 6% higher odds. The estimate is not statistically distinguishable from no association at conventional levels. This result is only illustrative because the model omits the baseline adoption hazard. The displayed warning explains that adoption can change over time, so omitting the period variable `per` can attribute a common time trend to exposure. The next specification includes period indicators and individual characteristics and explicitly shows the one-period exposure lag:

```{r}
#| label: diffreg-2
model_adjusted <- suppressWarnings(diffreg(
  kfam_diffnet ~
    # Adding age and a factor for village
    age + factor(village) + factor(per) +
    # Lagged exposure that uses the alternative graph
    exposure(
        lags = 1,
        alt.graph = exp_age_homo_graph,
        valued = TRUE
        )
  ))

summary(model_adjusted)
```

Arguments can be passed to `exposure()` directly through the model formula. In the adjusted model, the age-homophilic exposure coefficient is 0.284 ($p = 0.53$). A 0.10 increase in this exposure corresponds to an estimated odds ratio of $\exp(0.10 \times 0.284) = 1.03$, but the confidence interval includes no association. We therefore do not find a statistically detectable association between lagged age-homophilic exposure and adoption under this specification.

Age is positively associated with adoption: each additional year of age corresponds to an estimated odds ratio of $\exp(0.056) = 1.06$, or about 6% higher odds. The coefficient for village 21 is -0.701, corresponding to an odds ratio of $\exp(-0.701) = 0.50$ relative to village 2. Thus, conditional on the other model terms, respondents in village 21 have approximately half the odds of adoption of respondents in village 2.

Individual period coefficients compare each period with the reference period and need not be statistically significant one at a time for time to matter jointly. We can test the period indicators as a group using a likelihood-ratio test:

```{r}
#| label: diffreg-period-test
drop1(model_adjusted, test = "Chisq")["factor(per)", ]
```

After removing the artificial terminal period, the joint likelihood-ratio test does not reject a constant baseline adoption hazard over the observed periods ($p = 0.72$). This differs from the analysis that incorrectly treated the forced terminal adoptions as observed events: those entries generated a very large period-11 coefficient and made the period indicators appear jointly significant. The revised result illustrates why censoring the terminal cases and removing period 11 are important.

More details about what happens when calling the `diffreg()` function can be found in the library's manual.

## Simulating diffusion networks

Diffusion processes in networks are simulated using `rdiffnet()`, which supports options such as graph topology, threshold levels, the proportion of initial adopters, the centrality of those seeds, and the number of time steps. The simulation algorithm is as follows:

1. If there is no graph data, a baseline graph is created,

2. the initial adopters are identified,

3. a threshold value is assigned to each node,

4. if required, a set of $t$ networks is created, and

5. new adopters are selected at times $t > 1$ based on each node's exposure at time $t-1$. If that exposure exceeds the node's threshold, the node adopts; otherwise, it remains a non-adopter.

The function has only two mandatory arguments: the number of nodes (`n`) and the number of time steps (`t`). By default, it generates a scale-free graph with random rewiring at each time step, sets the proportion of initial adopters to 0.05, and draws a threshold for each node from a uniform distribution. This example shows the default settings for a diffusion process with 200 nodes and 10 time steps:

```{r}
#| label: simulating-adoption-process-1
#| eval: false
diffnet_1 <- rdiffnet(
  # Mandatory arguments
  n = 200,
  t = 10,
  # Optional arguments
  seed.nodes     = "random",
  seed.p.adopt   = 0.05,
  seed.graph     = "scale-free",
  rgraph.args    = list(),
  rewire         = TRUE,
  rewire.args    = list(),
  threshold.dist = runif(n),
  exposure.args  = list(),
  name           = "A diffusion network",
  behavior       = "Random contagion",
  stop.no.diff   = TRUE,
  disadopt       = NULL
)
```

This is equivalent to calling `rdiffnet(200, 10)`:

```{r}
#| label: simulating-adoption-process-call
#| eval: false
set.seed(331)
rdiffnet(200, 10)
```

Since the simulation process is inherently random, we use the function `set.seed()` to ensure reproducibility.

::: {.callout-tip}
Although the threshold model is deterministic conditional on its inputs, `rdiffnet()` calls `runif()` to generate threshold values by default, making the overall simulation stochastic. With fixed thresholds, a fixed network, and fixed seed nodes, it would be deterministic.
:::

`rdiffnet()` supports thresholds specified as a fixed value for all nodes, a vector of node-specific values, or a function. The proportion of initial adopters (`seed.p.adopt`) is used together with `seed.nodes`. Supported character values for `seed.nodes` are `"random"`, `"central"`, and `"marginal"`. If a vector of node indices is supplied instead, `rdiffnet()` ignores `seed.p.adopt` and uses those nodes as the initial adopters.

The `rdiffnet()` function also supports the use of a pre-defined graph as input. The following code shows how to simulate a diffusion process using a Watts-Strogatz graph:

```{r}
#| label: simulating-adoption-process-2
# Creating a graph based on the Watts-Strogatz model
set.seed(121)
graph <- rgraph_ws(200, 10, p = .3)

# Run the simulation
diffnet_2 <- rdiffnet(
  t              = 10,
  seed.graph     = graph,
  seed.p.adopt   = 0.1,
  threshold.dist = runif(200, .3, .5)
)
```

Since we are passing an actual network to the `seed.graph` argument, the `n` argument is no longer needed.


## Multiadoption

Starting with version 1.23.0, **netdiffuseR** supports simulating multi- and dis-adoption diffusion processes. To study a multi-adoption process, you can pass a `list` as the `seed.p.adopt` parameter. Here is a simple example:

```{r}
#| label: simulation-multiadoption-process-3
set.seed(1231)

diffnet_3 <- rdiffnet(
  200, 10,
  seed.p.adopt = list(0.1, 0.15),
  seed.nodes   = list("random", "random"),
  behavior     = list("Behavior 1", "Behavior 2")
)

diffnet_3
```

The output identifies the calculation as a multi-diffusion simulation and reports two behaviors, along with a final prevalence for each. The warning about coercing simulated times of adoption to integers is expected because the simulation uses discrete time; no information is lost. We display and explain these diagnostics here. In subsequent simulation chunks, we suppress the same repeated message and warning. `rdiffnet()` simulates as many behaviors as there are entries in the `seed.p.adopt` list.

::: {.callout-tip}
In the current implementation of `rdiffnet()`, the multi-adoption module simulates behaviors independently. That is, the code above would be equivalent to simulating the same behavior twice. More complicated models in which behaviors are interdependent are supported via the dis-adoption parameter.
:::

`rdiffnet()`'s defaults will replicate the simulation parameters across behaviors. Nonetheless, we can use lists to specify different parameters for each behavior. For example, the following code simulates two behaviors with different initial adopters, threshold distributions, seed nodes, and labels for the behaviors:

```{r}
#| label: simulation-multiadoption-process-4
set.seed(1232)
diffnet_4 <- suppressMessages(suppressWarnings(rdiffnet(
  200, 10,
  seed.p.adopt = list(0.1, 0.15),
  threshold.dist = list(
    runif(200, .3, .5),
    runif(200, .2, .4)
  ),
  seed.nodes = list("central", "random"),
  behavior   = list("tobacco", "alcohol")
)))

diffnet_4
```

In this particular example, we ran `rdiffnet()` with most of the parameters being in a `list`. The reader is invited to look at other types of possible inputs in the `rdiffnet()` documentation.

As in the previous section, we can provide a specific network as input. Besides fixed networks such as the small-world example, `rdiffnet()` supports `diffnet` objects. It then uses the object's graph as the seed graph and its observed periods as the simulation time points. Here is an example using the Korean Family Planning network:

```{r}
#| label: simulation-multiadoption-process-5
set.seed(1233)
diffnet_5 <- suppressMessages(suppressWarnings(rdiffnet(
  seed.graph     = kfam_diffnet,
  seed.p.adopt   = list(0.1, 0.15),
  seed.nodes     = list("random", "random"),
  threshold.dist = runif(nvertices(kfam_diffnet), .3, .5),
  behavior       = list("Behavior 1", "Behavior 2")
)))

diffnet_5
```

To visualize a diffusion process with more than one behavior, `split_behaviors()` separates the object into one `diffnet` object per behavior. We then use `plot_adopters()` for each behavior and `par()` to arrange both plots in a single window:

```{r}
#| label: simulation-multiadoption-process-5-plot
diffnets_5 <- split_behaviors(diffnet_5)
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), cex = .8)
plot_adopters(diffnets_5[[1]], main = "Behavior 1")
plot_adopters(diffnets_5[[2]], main = "Behavior 2")
par(op)
```

Notice the `op` object that stores the original graphical parameters. We use it to reset the graphical parameters after plotting the two behaviors.

## Disadoption

The disadoption feature introduced in netdiffuseR version 1.23.0 enables the study of diffusion processes in which adoption can be reversed. Disadoption is important for studying competition between products or beliefs [@lehmann_disadoption_2017]. The `disadopt` argument of `rdiffnet()` accepts a user-defined disadoption function, supporting tests of theoretical models for disadoption [@alipour_enough_2024]. Such a function must satisfy three requirements:

1. It must be a function that receives three arguments: `expo`, `cumadopt`, and `time`.

2. It must return one vector per behavior, identifying the nodes that drop each behavior. For example, if only node 5 drops the first of three behaviors, it should return `list(5L, integer(), integer())`.

3. If no nodes disadopt any of the $n$ behaviors, the function must return a list of $n$ empty integer vectors: `replicate(n, integer(), simplify = FALSE)`.

A template for a disadoption function, which currently returns no disadoption, follows:

```{r}
#| label: template-disadoption
#| eval: false
disadoption_function <- function(expo, cumadopt, time) {
  replicate(dim(cumadopt)[3], integer(), simplify = FALSE)
}
```

The following code shows how to build a disadoption function that randomly selects 10% of the adopters at time `t - 1`:

```{r}
#| label: disadoption-example-1-setup
random_dis <- function(expo, cumadopt, time) {

  # Number of behaviors
  num_of_behaviors <- dim(cumadopt)[3]

  # Making room for the disadopted nodes
  list_disadopt <- replicate(
    num_of_behaviors,
    integer(),
    simplify = FALSE
  )
  
  # Iterating through the behaviors
  for (q in 1:num_of_behaviors) {

    # Identifying the adopters at time t-1
    adopters_old <- which(cumadopt[, time - 1, q] == 1)

    if (length(adopters_old) != 0) {

      # Selecting 10% of adopters to disadopt
      list_disadopt[[q]] <- sample(
        adopters_old,
        ceiling(0.10 * length(adopters_old)
        )
      )

    }

  }

  list_disadopt

}
```

It is worth highlighting a few things from the code:

1. The `expo` argument is the entire exposure *array*. This means that it has three dimensions: the first dimension is the number of nodes, the second is the number of time points, and the third is the number of behaviors.

2. The `cumadopt` argument is the cumulative adoption array. It has the same dimensions as `expo`. The value of `cumadopt[i, t, q]` is 1 if node `i` has adopted behavior `q` at time `t`.

3. The `time` argument is the current time point in the simulation. This allows the function to know when the disadopt function is being called.

4. The code `which(cumadopt[, time - 1, q] == 1)` identifies the nodes whose `cumadopt` entry equals 1 at time $t - 1$.

To simulate a diffusion process with disadoption, we can use the `rdiffnet()` function as follows:

```{r}
#| label: disadoption-example-1
set.seed(1234)
diffnet_6  <- rdiffnet(
  seed.graph   = graph,
  t            = 10,
  disadopt     = random_dis,
  seed.p.adopt = 0.1
  )

diffnet_6
```

Using a `disadopt` function, we can build more complex models with competing behaviors. For instance, the following rule prevents nodes from retaining both behaviors simultaneously by making double adopters drop behavior 1:

$$
\text{Disadopt 1}_{it} = \left\{\begin{array}{l}Yes,\quad\text{If behavior 2 has adopted}\\\text{No},\quad\text{otherwise.}\end{array}\right.
$$

The following code shows how to build such a function:

```{r}
#| label: disadoption-example-2-fun
one_only <- function(expo, cumadopt, time) {

  # Identifying double adopters
  ids <- which(apply(cumadopt[, time, ], 1, sum) == 2)

  if (length(ids) == 0)
    return(list(integer(), integer()))

  # Otherwise, make them pick one (in this case, we prefer the second)
  list(ids, integer())

}
```

Of the code above, we can highlight the following:

1. We identify the number of behaviors adopted by each individual at time `t` using `apply(cumadopt[, time, ], 1, sum)`. In a two-behavior model, this returns 0 for no adoption, 1 for one behavior, or 2 for both behaviors.

2. The `which()` function is used to identify the nodes adopting both behaviors (after calling `apply()`).

3. If there are no double adopters, the function returns a list with empty vectors.

Let's simulate a diffusion process with the disadoption function `one_only`:

```{r}
#| label: disadoption-example-2
set.seed(331)
diffnet_7 <- suppressMessages(suppressWarnings(rdiffnet(
  200, 10,
  disadopt     = one_only,
  seed.p.adopt = list(0.1, 0.1),
  seed.nodes   = list("random", "random"),
  behavior     = list("Behavior 1", "Behavior 2")
)))
diffnet_7
```

Finally, we can demonstrate that each node adopted at most one behavior by taking the cumulative adoption matrix at the last time point and checking whether any node adopted both. The `toa_mat()` function extracts the adoption matrices from the model:

```{r}
#| label: checking-if-worked
toas <- toa_mat(diffnet_7)

# Putting the two behaviors together
adopted <-  cbind(
  toas[[1]]$cumadopt[, 10],
  toas[[2]]$cumadopt[, 10]
)

# Looking at the first 5
head(adopted, 5)

# Tabulating side by side
table(adopted[, 1], adopted[, 2])
```

As expected, there's no entry in the table in which both behaviors were adopted by the same node. Using the `disadopt` function, we can build (and study) increasingly complex models of network diffusion.

# Conclusion

This paper has introduced the netdiffuseR R package, which facilitates the estimation and simulation of contagion and diffusion processes on networks. The tutorial provides reproducible examples that readers can adapt to the classical datasets included with the package or to their own data. Its empirical sections demonstrate the calculation and interpretation of network exposure, including extensions based on structural equivalence, attributes, and homophily. Its simulation sections provide tools for theoretical testing of diffusion processes.

We also provide examples of multi-diffusion processes in which more than one idea or behavior spreads through a network. The Korean Family Planning study, for example, records multiple family-planning choices over time. The disadoption examples show how to represent processes in which an individual adopts a behavior, subsequently discontinues it, and may later resume it. Although few available datasets capture these dynamics in detail, the package supplies tools for studying them as such data become available.

We hope that by providing these illustrative examples, others will be able to use netdiffuseR in their work. Diffusion processes are ubiquitous in science and everyday life. The diffusion paradigm was first established by Ryan and Gross in 1943 [@valente_origins_1995] but it continues to grow and evolve, and our hope is that this publication will further encourage both growth and evolution.
